Speed bin distributions for FleetDNA single-unit short-haul vehicles by hour Figure 21 shows the distribution of time spent in speed bins for refuse trucks from FleetDNA, which were logged operating on urban roads. For some early morning hours, we see a high proportion of time spent at 60 mph on weekdays. For urban other roads on weekdays, the primary peak is spent at a slow 5 mph, perhaps because the trucks are frequently stopping on urban trash pickup routes. On other roads on weekends, as well as freeways on weekdays, we see slightly more sporadic speed bin distributions due to lower data density, but also some hours of the day hitting 40% of their time at a slow 5 mph as well. For most hours of the day, refuse trucks are not driving very fast. 33 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 21. Speed bin distributions for FleetDNA refuse trucks by hour Figure 22 shows the speed bin distributions for transit buses in the FleetDNA database. Buses on urban freeways spend time fairly evenly across speed bins between 0 and 40 mph, leading into a mild peak around 60 mph. Early morning hours have a stronger high-speed peak, but this feature is probably mostly due to less available data during those hours. Across all hours, urban other roads have a clear low-speed peak around 10–15 mph, with tails extending to 0 and 30 mph. Figure 22. Figure 23 displays the available speed bin distributions based on FleetDNA school buses, which drove on urban other roads on weekdays. Some midday hours (hour IDs 10, 11, and 12) had very low data and contribute to some of the observed spikes on the chart. Aside from those, we do see some low-speed trends with a main broad peak centered around 15 mph and extending to 0 and 30 mph. There is a slight secondary peak around 45 mph for hours 6 and 16 in the legend (hour IDs 7 and 17). Hour line 17 (hour ID 18) also had more sporadic and less smooth behavior, spending 30%–40% of its time in three disparate speed bins centered at 20, 35, and 60 mph. Possibly, we can use hour ID 8 (hour 7) as a proxy for all school bus hours due to this hour having the most logged data out of the minimal school bus data available. Alternatively, hour IDs 8, 9, and 13–17 had tighter bounds on their uncertainty in the average speed section of the paper, and those distributions could perhaps be used, with hours outside of these filled with the closest hour of sufficient data.
